posts.title: “I don't like it”: three questions that turn it into a change
posts.hook: “I don't like it” is a feeling, and nobody can edit a feeling.
posts.caption:
“I don't like it” is a feeling, and nobody can edit a feeling.
Whoever carries feedback from a brand to a creator has to turn it into a change first.

Passed on as it is, that line costs a full round. The creator guesses, changes four things, and the one thing that bothered the reviewer is still in the cut.

So before feedback leaves my desk, I put three questions to it.

Where? The exact seconds. “The opening” is too loose. “0:02 to 0:05” is usable.

What? The thing on screen or in the audio at that moment. A line, a shot, the music, the pace.

Compared to what? Every “I don't like it” has a picture behind it of what the person expected. Ask for that picture: an older ad, a reference, a line in the brief.

Then write the note as an instruction. “At 0:03, swap the product shot for the line to camera, like the reference in the brief.”

If I cannot write it that way, the feedback is not ready to send. I go back to the reviewer, not forward to the creator.

A creator can act on a timestamp. A mood only gets a guess.

posts.title: Creator work runs on WhatsApp: four habits that make the chat a workflow
posts.hook: Creator work in India runs on WhatsApp. No tool will change that.
posts.caption:
Creator work in India runs on WhatsApp. No tool will change that.
So the useful question for a brand team is how to make a chat behave like a workflow.

The usual advice is to move creators into your project tool. A creator working with several brands will not keep a separate login for each one. They will reply where they already are.

Four habits make the chat do most of a tracker's work.

1. One group per campaign. Put the brand and the go-live date in the group name.

2. The brief is one pinned message. Must-haves first, as a numbered list, so a creator can reply “point 3 is not clear”.

3. One ask per message. Three asks in one paragraph get one answer.

4. Voice notes are fine for talking. Every decision gets typed back in one line: “Confirming: shoot on Thursday, opening option 2.”

Then the step that happens outside the chat. At the end of each day, every decision and every date moves into one tracker the brand can open.

The chat is where the work gets done. The tracker is where the client reads it.

Meet creators where they already work, and keep the record where the brand can find it.

posts.title: AI made the draft fast. The wait has moved to approvals
posts.hook: AI can make a first cut in minutes.
posts.caption:
AI can make a first cut in minutes.
The approval still needs the same people and the same days.

For a brand team wondering what AI changes in creative work, this is the part to plan for: the making got shorter, so the waiting is now the longest stage.

When a video took a week to make, two days in someone's inbox went unnoticed. When it takes a morning, those two days are most of the timeline.

Three things are worth agreeing before anyone generates anything.

One named person per approval stage. A team inbox does not say yes. A person does.

What each person is reading for. Legal reads the claim. The brand lead reads the tone. Nobody reopens what someone else has cleared.

A reply-by time, and what happens when it passes.

Some of the work stays with people for a plain reason. The context that decides an approval is often written nowhere a model can read it: a claim that was pulled last quarter, a word the founder never wants on screen. A person has to carry that into the review.

A fast draft only helps if the yes can keep up with it.

posts.title: Brief to Live: a creator campaign day in under a minute
posts.hook: A creator campaign day is four check-ins around the shoot.
posts.caption:
A creator campaign day is four check-ins around the shoot.

Morning: the brief goes out with the must-haves at the top.

Midday: questions come back. If two creators ask the same thing, the brief has a hole, so the brief gets fixed and then the replies go out.

Afternoon: first cuts. Claim, product and ask get checked before the brand sees anything.

Evening: a follow-up by voice note, and every decision from the chat goes into one tracker.

The one to copy tomorrow is the midday rule. The same question twice is a note about your brief.

This is Brief to Live, a series on what happens between the brief and the ad going live.

posts.title: Myth and fact: “AI made it” does not lower the QC bar
posts.hook: “AI made it” is never a reason to lower the bar.
posts.caption:
“AI made it” is never a reason to lower the bar.
The person scrolling past your ad has no idea how it was made, and would not care if they did.

The myth is that an AI video deserves a lighter check because it was quick and cheap. The fact runs the other way. It needs the same check as any creator video, and three more.

The same for every video, whoever made it:
Is the claim the approved claim, word for word?
Is the product shown the way it really looks?
Is the ask clear in the last seconds?

Extra for AI:
The pack. Letters on the label, the logo shape and the pack colour drift in generated footage. Pause on every frame where the product is close.
Hands, faces and on-screen text, at the moments they move.
The voice. Listen to how it says the brand name and any Indian word.

If a video fails one line, it goes back. No discount for the tool.

Here is what AI does change. A remake is quick. That is a reason to reject more often, since saying no now costs an hour and not a week.

The bar belongs to the brand, and the tool does not get a vote.

posts.title: Brief to Live: four extra takes that save a reshoot
posts.hook: Most people see the ad. Almost nobody sees the shoot day.
posts.caption:
Most people see the ad. Almost nobody sees the shoot day.

A reshoot is usually decided on the shoot itself, by what did not get filmed.

So the plan for the day carries four extra takes besides the main one:

1. Three openings for the same script, because the opening is the first thing to test.
2. The product up close, label readable, held still.
3. The approved claim, word for word, in one clean take. An edit cannot repair a paraphrased claim.
4. Ten seconds of the room with nobody talking, to cover cuts.

Tick all four before the creator packs up. After that, each missing one is a second shoot day.

Brief to Live is a series on what happens between the brief and the ad going live.

posts.title: AI output needs rounds: what to say on the first call
posts.hook: AI creative needs a few rounds. Say so on the first call.
posts.caption:
AI creative needs a few rounds. Say so on the first call.
A client who expects a finished film in round one will read every later round as a failure.

With the first briefs of the year going out this week, here is how I set it up on that call. Each round gets a name and one job.

Round one is direction. One question only: is this the right idea, look and voice? Small flaws are expected here and nobody lists them.

Round two is accuracy. Product, pack, claim and on-screen text.

Round three is polish. Timing, sound and subtitles.

Then the rule that protects the dates. A note belongs to its round. A change of idea in round three sends us back to round one, and the go-live date moves with it. Said on day one, that is a plan. Said in week three, it sounds like an excuse.

After the call, it goes in writing: the rounds, what each is for, and who replies by when.

This matters more with AI because round one arrives so fast. People then expect the final cut at the same speed.

Rounds stop feeling like rework when everyone was told they were coming.

posts.title: One script, five variations: each changes one thing
posts.hook: One script, five variations. Each variation changes exactly one thing.
posts.caption:
One script, five variations. Each variation changes exactly one thing.

The easy way to brief variations is to change everything at once: new opening, new creator, new music, new ask. Five ads come back, one does better, and nobody can say which change did it.

Keep the script fixed. Change one of five things per variation: the opening, the person, the setting, the format or the ask. Name each variation in the brief and use the same name on the file and the ad.

One caution. The variations have to look different at a glance, or they compete with each other.

The next step is to put these on a calendar. Decoded #11 shows how.

posts.title: Feedback that repeats should become a rule in the brief
posts.hook: The second time you give the same feedback, stop giving it.
posts.caption:
The second time you give the same feedback, stop giving it.
Write it down as a rule and put it at the top of the next brief.

Every brand has notes that come back campaign after campaign. Show the logo early. Product in the hand, never on a table. Each time one returns as feedback, the team pays for a round the last campaign already paid for.

Here is the method for anyone who reviews creator work.

Keep one running list per brand and call it Rules.

When a note shows up a second time, move it from the feedback thread into that list. Use the reviewer's own words and add the date.

Paste the list at the top of every new brief. Check a first cut against it before anyone gives an opinion.

Once a quarter, ask the brand which rules no longer hold and delete them. A list that only grows stops getting read.

This is the small, manual version of what we call Brand Memory at Galvor. Plenty of data, no memory is how one note ends up written six times.

Every ad should make the next one better. So should every round of feedback.

posts.title: Five questions before any campaign starts
posts.hook: Before any campaign starts, I ask five questions.
posts.caption:
Before any campaign starts, I ask five questions.

If one of them has no answer, the brief is not ready.

1. Who exactly is this for?
2. What is the one thing they should do?
3. What did the last campaign teach us?
4. What must be said, and what must never be?
5. Who says yes, and by when?

The third one gets skipped most easily, and it is the one that makes this campaign better than the last.

With Republic Day sales closing and new financial year plans opening, this is a good week to run your next brief past all five. The slides have what a good answer looks like for each.

posts.title: Must-fix vs preference: sort feedback before it goes to the creator
posts.hook: Every round of feedback needs two columns: must-fix and preference.
posts.caption:
Every round of feedback needs two columns: must-fix and preference.
Without them, a creator treats a passing thought and a legal problem as the same size.

Feedback usually arrives as one long list. The reviewer knows which lines are serious. The creator does not, so they either change everything or pick the easy ones.

The test I use to sort a note:

Must-fix means it breaks the brief, the brand rules or the law. A changed claim. The product not visible. The wrong pack. A missing paid partnership label.

Preference means “I would have done it differently”. The music, a word, the colour of a shirt.

Then three steps before anything is sent.

Must-fix notes go first, numbered, each with a timestamp.

Preferences go below, marked “only if it is easy”.

When notes arrive mixed, I ask the reviewer one question: which of these stops us from going live?

That question does most of the sorting. Most lists have fewer must-fix lines than their length suggests.

Share the two columns with the brand as well. It heads off the late “but I asked for that”.

A creator who knows what has to change can change it in one pass.

posts.title: “We need AI videos”: three questions that turn it into a brief
posts.hook: “We need AI videos” is a request about the tool.
posts.caption:
“We need AI videos” is a request about the tool.
It says how you want the videos made and leaves out what to make.

Three questions turn that sentence into a brief a team can work from. The first is where the videos will run.

1. Where will it run? Name the placement, since a platform name is too wide. A Reels ad, a product page video and a marketplace listing video are three different films. Length, shape and how early the product must appear all follow from the answer.

2. What must it do there? One job. Stop a new buyer mid-scroll, answer a doubt for someone comparing, or bring a past buyer back.

3. What will it run next to? This one gets skipped. If the new video looks like the ads already running, it competes with your own work. In Galvor's analysis of video ads launched May to Sep 2026, new ads that looked like many running ads got 36% less first-month spend.

Only after these three does the making question come up. Sometimes AI is the right way to make it. Sometimes a creator in her own kitchen is.

Decide the job first. How it gets made is the last line of the brief.

posts.title: The no-surprise rule: a five-line message for bad news
posts.hook: Bad news costs least on the day you find it.
posts.caption:
Bad news costs least on the day you find it.
My rule in client servicing is that a client should never learn about a delay from the deadline.

A creator falls ill. A first cut fails the check. A date starts to slip. The pull is to fix it quietly and report afterwards. If the fix works, nobody knows. If it does not, the client has less time and less reason to trust the next update.

So the message goes the same day, in writing, and it has five lines.

What happened. One sentence, no cushioning.

What it affects. The date, the deliverable, or nothing yet.

What I have already done about it.

What I need from you, if anything.

When you will hear from me next.

The third and fifth lines carry the most weight. They tell the client that someone is already on it and that they do not need to chase.

Write it even when the fix is already under way. An update that turns out to be unnecessary costs two minutes.

A problem the client heard about early is one you solve together. A problem they find on their own is one they hold against you.
